title: KfW-backed biomass heating in Serbian towns delivers four of ten plants
programme: Promotion of Renewable Energy – Development of the Biomass Market in Serbia
problem: Serbian municipal district heating companies burned fossil fuels and needed a renewable heat source.
solution: German development bank KfW and the Swiss government financed a switch of municipal heating plants from fossil fuels to wood biomass, with financing agreements signed in 2017. A second phase was signed with the European Commission and the German government in May 2024.
implementer: Municipal district heating companies in Serbia, supported by KfW and GIZ
funding: Phase 1 was financed by KfW and the Swiss government; phase 2 agreements worth EUR 31.9 million in grants and loans were signed in May 2024 by the European Commission, KfW and the German government.
results: By May 2024 four plants (Priboj, Mali Zvornik, Novi Pazar, Majdanpek) were complete, although the EUR 27 million first phase was meant to cover ten. In July 2024, 41 environmental organisations asked KfW to suspend the programme over forest, climate and air impacts.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own flagship programme for switching municipal heat networks to biomass with KfW and EU money. Its slow delivery is a direct warning for the second phase, expected to cover Niš, Bajina Bašta, Prijepolje, Novi Pazar and Rača.
adapt_needed: Size each plant to verified, sustainable local wood supply and favour heat pumps, solar thermal or geothermal where supply is uncertain.
blockers: Limited sustainable wood, competition with households for fuelwood and weak forest data and enforcement.
quote: By May 2024, four biomass district heating plants in Serbia, located in Priboj, Mali Zvornik, Novi Pazar, and Majdanpek, had been completed

title: Banja Luka's EBRD-funded biomass heating plant hit by fuel shortages
programme: EBRD Green Cities Framework – Banja Luka District Heating
problem: Banja Luka's district heating ran on heavy fuel oil and needed a cleaner fuel.
solution: In 2017 the EBRD helped finance a 49 MWth wood-biomass heating plant, run by Eko Toplane, with wood bought from forest concessionaires.
implementer: Eko Toplane, owned 51% by IEE Banja Luka and 49% by the City of Banja Luka
funding: A 16.4 million investment including an EBRD loan of EUR 8.3 million, later propped up by city subsidies.
results: Supply fell 58 per cent short of demand in the 2022 season and the city paid BAM 7 million (around EUR 3.5 million) in subsidies between 2022 and May 2024. Heating costs still rose 23 per cent in 2023-4, and 140 users asked to disconnect in the first five months of 2024.
serbia_reason: Serbian towns are planning similar development-bank-financed switches from fuel oil to wood biomass. Banja Luka shows the supply, price and subsidy risks of that model next door.
adapt_needed: Secure long-term, verified biomass supply and stress-test heat tariffs before financing, or choose non-biomass heat sources.
blockers: An unstable, partly illegal wood market and municipal budgets that cannot keep covering operating losses.
quote: Since 2018, the company operating the plant, Eko Toplane, has faced severe issues with the regularity and consistency of biomass delivery. This problem culminated in a 58 per cent gap between supply and demand for the 2022 season.

title: Converting Tuzla coal unit to biomass would need far more land
problem: An old coal-fired unit at the Tuzla power plant, which produces both power and heat, needs replacing.
solution: In 2022 the entity-owned utility Elektroprivreda BiH and the EBRD agreed to consider converting Unit 3 to burn willow from short-rotation plantations on former mine land, plus waste incineration.
funding: The EBRD signed a mandate letter in September 2022 to consider financing; no amount is reported.
results: EPBiH plans 1,075 hectares of willow at former mines, but Biofuelwatch estimates 6,042 hectares would be needed, 5.6 times more. Bankwatch judges the plan will not cut BiH's climate impact significantly and is not viable.
serbia_reason: Serbia's state utility also runs ageing lignite units, some of which supply heat to nearby towns. Tuzla shows how badly fuel and land needs can be underestimated when converting coal units to biomass.
adapt_needed: Base any coal-unit conversion on an independent assessment of sustainable feedstock and compare it with heat pumps, solar thermal and storage.
blockers: Too little sustainable biomass and weak forest governance to fuel a large converted unit.
quote: However, this plan will not help reduce BiH’s climate impact significantly and will require much more land for the SRC plantations than currently projected.

title: Serbia alone in Western Balkans to transpose RED II biomass criteria
programme: RED II biomass sustainability and GHG saving criteria
problem: Biomass counted as renewable must meet sustainability rules, but Western Balkan countries were slow to adopt the EU criteria due by the end of 2022.
solution: Serbia transposed the RED II sustainability and greenhouse gas saving criteria for biomass into national law, as the Energy Community requires.
results: Serbia is the only Western Balkan country to have transposed the criteria, yet its forest biomass use of 18.5 TWh in 2023 is already close to the estimated 19.4 TWh of natural growth. Bankwatch also considers the RED II criteria themselves insufficient.
serbia_reason: Serbia already has the legal criteria in place. The gap is enforcement and reliable forest data, not law.
adapt_needed: Back the criteria with independent forest inventories and monitoring of wood sources for heat plants.
blockers: Illegal logging, survey-based consumption data and no valid strategic forestry plans.
quote: Of the Western Balkan countries, only Serbia has transposed the RED II sustainability and GHG saving criteria for biomass into its national legislation, while Montenegro and Kosovo have partially done so, but need to adopt implementing legislation.

title: Serbia's wood export curbs and price caps only partly protected consumers
programme: Wood export quotas, pellet trade restrictions and retail price caps (2022–2024)
problem: The 2021–2022 energy crisis sent fuelwood and pellet prices soaring while exports became highly profitable.
solution: Serbia set export quotas for raw wood (August 2022 to February 2023), restricted pellet exports (December 2022 to January 2023), capped retail prices and in April 2024 banned pellet imports.
results: Regional fuelwood and pellet export volumes fell 20.3 and 19 per cent in 2022, but prices in some cases stayed too high for local people. Serbia saw a large drop in pellet consumption as public trust in price stability fell.
serbia_reason: This was Serbia's own response to a biomass price shock. It shows ad-hoc trade and price controls do not create a stable biomass market for households or heat plants.
adapt_needed: Pair any future price measures with targeted support for energy-poor households and a shift to non-biomass heating.
blockers: Volatile regional wood markets, illegal logging and unreliable consumption data.
quote: Although these measures were aimed at protecting local consumers, prices in some cases remained too high for the local population, leading them into energy poverty.

title: Serbia's planned biomass district heating would use almost all spare wood
programme: Serbia NECP 2024 – biomass in district heating
problem: Serbia's district heating relies heavily on fossil gas and the country must raise its renewable share under Energy Community 2030 targets.
solution: The July 2024 NECP plans more biomass and some solar heat in district heating, and towns have lined up biomass heating projects to 2030.
implementer: Government of Serbia and municipal district heating companies
results: An EBRD assessment found only 33.6 ktoe (390.4 GWh) of wood left after existing uses, and biomass heating projects planned to 2030 (369.67 GWh) would use almost all of it. The NECP itself cites limited sustainable wood as one reason Serbia cannot meet its 2030 Energy Community renewables target.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's current national plan for heat under its Energy Community targets. The evidence shows biomass cannot be the main route to cleaner district heating.
adapt_needed: Shift planned biomass capacity towards heat pumps, solar thermal, geothermal, seasonal storage and building efficiency.
blockers: Unreliable forest data, illegal logging and households' heavy dependence on fuelwood.
quote: Recent data confirms that towns in Serbia cannot rely on woody biomass for additional district heating needs.
